claims.text: The investigated particles are sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles produced by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The as-produced nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
The as-produced AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles initially exhibit a single-phase FCC structure.
Sluggish diffusion is overridden in nanoscale AuCoCuNiPt by active, element-specific diffusion.
Au and Cu are the relevant low-melting-point elements in this quinary alloy.
Surface-energy gradients and local surface lattice distortion lower the migration barriers of Au and Cu relative to bulk diffusion.
The proposed surface-diffusion mechanism becomes dominant at approximately 600 K.
For sub-10 nm particles, the thermodynamic driving force from high surface free energy exceeds entropic stabilization.
Au and Cu have lower surface energies than the other alloy components and therefore segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
After segregation, Au and Cu have higher diffusivities and lower evaporation temperatures than the remaining components.
Surface segregation of Au and Cu causes their depletion from the core and subsequent evaporation.
Heating produces a progressive widening of the nanoparticle size distribution.
Heating changes elliptical or icosahedral particles into spherical particles to reduce surface area.
Preferential Au and Cu loss shifts the particles away from equiatomic composition and destabilizes the FCC structure, potentially causing transformation or dissolution.
The segregation, evaporation, and possible FCC destabilization occur significantly below the bulk melting point.
The mechanism is strictly valid below 10 nm because surface-energy terms dominate at that scale.
The mechanism fails in bulk material and in particles larger than 50 nm, where bulk thermodynamics and sluggish diffusion prevail.
Existing nanoscale thermodynamic data are insufficient to fix the critical temperature, and the silicon nitride substrate may affect diffusion kinetics.

Surface enrichment and core depletion can be tested by temperature-resolved in situ STEM elemental mapping and compared with atomistic simulations that alter kinetic barriers while retaining surface-energy terms.

The hypothesis is falsified if heating above the proposed threshold produces no Au/Cu surface segregation, or if simulations show that the imposed kinetic barrier prevents segregation and evaporation despite surface-energy gradients.

contradictions.description: The causal account invokes both local lattice distortion and temperature-dependent kinetic-barrier crossing, while the proposed test is framed as determining whether surface-energy gradients alone explain phase separation. Unless lattice distortion and kinetic effects are independently controlled, the experiment does not isolate the stated sole cause.
